title: Great Books · Episode 1
chapters: Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction

units.t: Great Books. Episode one.
In this episode: The great epics, Shakespeare, The rise of the novel and Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction.
Part one. The great epics.
Long before novels or films, people gathered to hear poems about heroes, gods and monsters.
Some of those poems are still read, performed and argued over thousands of years later.
What makes an epic.
An epic is a long story told in verse, centred on a hero whose deeds matter to a whole community or nation.
Epics usually feature gods or supernatural forces, great journeys or wars, and big questions about fate, honour and death.
Many began as oral poetry, performed from memory by professional singers long before anyone wrote them down.
Repeated phrases, like Homer's 'rosy-fingered Dawn', helped performers keep track of thousands of lines.
Scholars distinguish these traditional epics from later 'literary' epics, written by a single known author who deliberately imitated the old style.
Gilgamesh and Homer.
The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq.
Poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, were written in Sumerian around 4,000 years ago.
After his friend Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh searches for eternal life and fails.
When its tablets were found at Nineveh in the 1850s, George Smith's 1872 translation of a flood story strikingly similar to Noah's caused a sensation.
The Iliad, credited to Homer, covers only a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War, built around the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles.
It ends with the funeral of Hector, not the fall of Troy.
The Odyssey follows Odysseus on his ten-year journey home to Ithaca and his wife Penelope.
It gave English the word 'odyssey'.
The Aeneid.
The Roman poet Virgil wrote the Aeneid between about 29 and 19 BC, during the rule of Augustus, Rome's first emperor.

Deliberately echoing Homer, it follows Aeneas, a Trojan prince who escapes burning Troy and, after a tragic love affair with Queen Dido of Carthage, reaches Italy, where his descendants will found Rome.
The poem celebrates Rome's destiny but is haunted by the suffering that destiny demands.
Virgil died in 19 BC before finishing it and reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned.
Augustus refused, and the Aeneid became a cornerstone of Western education for nearly 2,000 years.
Mahabharata and Beowulf.
The Mahabharata, written in Sanskrit, is often called the longest poem in the world, with around 100,000 verses in its longest versions.
Attributed to the sage Vyasa, it grew over centuries.
It tells of a bitter family conflict ending in war at Kurukshetra.
Within it sits the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna about duty and action, sacred to hundreds of millions of Hindus.
Beowulf is the most famous poem in Old English.
Though set in Scandinavia, it was written in England, with estimates of its date ranging from about AD 700 to 1000.
Beowulf kills Grendel and Grendel's mother, then dies fighting a dragon.
It survives in one manuscript, scorched in a 1731 fire in London.
Why epics endure.
Epics survive because their questions never date: how to face death, what we owe our families and communities, whether glory is worth the cost.
Their story patterns are everywhere.
Joseph Campbell argued in 1949 that many myths share a 'hero's journey', an idea that influenced Star Wars, though scholars dispute how universal it is.
R.
R. Tolkien argued that Beowulf's monsters deserved to be taken seriously, and its echoes run through The Hobbit.
Oral storytelling is also a living tradition in Australia, where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have passed stories down over many generations.
To try an epic, start with a modern translation, such as Emily Wilson's 2017 Odyssey, or an audiobook.
These poems were made to be heard.
The key idea: An epic is a long verse story about a hero whose deeds matter to a whole community, and many began as oral poetry.
Part two. Shakespeare.
A glove-maker's son from a small market town wrote plays that are still performed around the world, and he put words in your mouth you didn't know were his.
A Stratford boy.
William Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564.
His father John was a glove-maker who became a local official.
At 18 William married Anne Hathaway, who was 26.
They had three children: Susanna, then twins Hamnet and Judith.
Hamnet died in 1596, aged 11.
Surprisingly little is known about his personal life, and the records have a gap from about 1585 to 1592 that scholars call 'the lost years'.
By 1592 he was working in London, where rival Robert Greene mocked him as an 'upstart crow'.
Unusually, he was actor, writer and part-owner of his company, which made him fairly wealthy.
The Globe and the Folio.
He became a leading member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, which became the King's Men after James I took the throne in 1603.
In 1599 the company built the Globe Theatre on the south bank of the Thames.
It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance set the thatched roof alight.
A reconstruction opened near the site in 1997.
Shakespeare is credited with about 37 plays and 154 sonnets.
Many plays were never printed in his lifetime.
In 1623 two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, published 36 of them in the First Folio.
About 18, including Macbeth and The Tempest, had never been printed and might otherwise have vanished.
About 235 copies survive, including one in Sydney's State Library of NSW.
Tragedy, comedy and history.
His tragedies follow powerful people destroyed by their own choices, flaws or circumstances.
Hamlet agonises over revenge.
Macbeth, spurred by a prophecy and his wife's ambition, spirals into tyranny.
Othello is manipulated by Iago into jealousy and murder.
King Lear divides his kingdom and is betrayed.
Characters think aloud in soliloquies, letting us overhear their minds.
The comedies, such as A Midsummer Night's Dream and Twelfth Night, feature mistaken identities, disguises and happy endings, usually weddings.
Because women could not act on the English stage, boys played female roles.
The histories, including Richard III and Henry V, shaped popular ideas of English kings far more than historians would like.
Late plays like The Tempest are often called romances: stories of loss, magic and forgiveness.
Words and verse.
The Oxford English Dictionary lists Shakespeare as the earliest known source for many words, such as 'eyeball', 'bedroom' and 'swagger', though some were probably already in speech.
Phrases first found in his plays include 'wild-goose chase', Romeo and Juliet, 'green-eyed monster' and 'a foregone conclusion', both Othello.
Much of his writing is blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter.
That is ten syllables with an unstressed-stressed beat, da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, close to natural speech.
Kings and lovers tend to speak in verse, servants and comic characters in prose.
A rhyming couplet often closes a scene, like a musical full stop.
Reading aloud makes the lines easier to follow.
Why he lasts.
Shakespeare's plays survive because they deal with things that never go away: ambition, jealousy, love, grief, power and family conflict.
They are also endlessly adaptable.
West Side Story reworks Romeo and Juliet, 10 Things I Hate About You updates The Taming of the Shrew, and The Lion King borrows from Hamlet.
Australian director Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet, 1996, kept the original language in a modern setting.
Bell Shakespeare, founded by John Bell in 1990, tours his plays around Australia.
The best way in is to watch a performance first.
These were scripts for actors, not texts for exams.
The key idea: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, became a London actor, writer and shareholder, and little is known of his private life.
Part three. The rise of the novel.
The novel is the youngest of the great literary forms, yet it became the way billions of people explore other lives.
Here's how it began, and the Australian books worth knowing.
The first novels.
A novel is a long, invented story told in prose, usually focused on characters' inner lives.
The word comes from the Italian 'novella', meaning a new story.
Around AD 1000 in Japan, the court lady Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, a subtle story of life at the imperial court.
It is often called the world's first novel, though 'first' depends on how strictly you define the form.
In Europe, the book most often called the first modern novel is Cervantes' Don Quixote, 1605 and 1615.
A gentleman reads so many chivalry tales that he becomes a knight and attacks windmills, believing them giants.
It gave English the word 'quixotic' and the phrase 'tilting at windmills'.
English novels take off.
Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, 1719, is often called the first English novel.
It presented itself as a true account of a sailor shipwrecked for 28 years, and its power came from practical detail.
Defoe was probably partly inspired by Alexander Selkirk, marooned off Chile from 1704 to 1709.
Richardson's Pamela, 1740, and Fielding's Tom Jones, 1749, followed.
The novel spread because several changes arrived together: cheaper printing, rising literacy, and a middle class with money and leisure.
Circulating libraries let readers borrow books for a fee, and many readers and writers were women.
Unlike epics about heroes, novels focused on ordinary people.
The form proved flexible, producing Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, 1818, an early science fiction work.
Austen and Dickens.
Jane Austen, 1775–1817, published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously, the first credited only to 'a Lady'.
Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death at 41.
Pride and Prejudice, 1813, opens with the famous line about a single man in possession of a good fortune.
She wrote about courtship, class and money with sharp irony, and refined a way of slipping in and out of a character's thoughts.
Charles Dickens, 1812–1870, was Victorian England's superstar novelist.
At 12, when his father was jailed for debt, he worked in a boot polish factory, an experience that fuelled his anger at poverty.
Most of his novels came out in weekly or monthly instalments, much like a TV series.
'Dickensian' now describes grim, overcrowded poverty.
Australia's classics.
Australian novels grew out of the colonial experience.
Marcus Clarke's For the Term of His Natural Life, first serialised in the early 1870s, told a harrowing story of the convict system.
Dickens's Great Expectations also features a convict transported to New South Wales.
Miles Franklin's My Brilliant Career, 1901, about a spirited young woman in the bush, was written when she was very young, and her bequest later funded the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
Henry Handel Richardson was the pen name of Ethel Richardson, author of The Getting of Wisdom.
Patrick White, author of Voss and The Tree of Man, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973.
He was the first Australian to win it.
Modern Australian voices.
Tim Winton has won the Miles Franklin Award four times.
His novel Cloudstreet, 1991, about two working-class families sharing a big old house in Perth, is often voted a favourite Australian book.
Kate Grenville's The Secret River, 2005, follows a convict settler on the Hawkesbury River and confronts the violence of colonisation.
Kim Scott, a Noongar writer, became the first Aboriginal author to win the Miles Franklin, for Benang in 2000.
Waanyi writer Alexis Wright won it for Carpentaria in 2007.
To start reading, pick one classic and one modern novel, and try your local library's free audiobook and ebook apps.
The key idea: The novel is long prose fiction about characters' inner lives, with early landmarks in Japan's Tale of Genji and Spain's Don Quixote.
Part four. Frankenstein and the birth of science fiction.
A teenager, a stormy summer and a ghost story contest produced one of the most influential novels ever written.
The year without summer.
In April 1815, Mount Tambora in what is now Indonesia exploded in one of the largest eruptions in recorded history.
Its ash and gases cooled the global climate, and Europe's 1816 became the year without a summer, with cold, rain and failed harvests.

That June, a group of young English writers stayed near Lake Geneva: the poet Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati, and nearby Percy Bysshe Shelley, eighteen-year-old Mary Godwin, her stepsister Claire Clairmont and Byron's doctor, John Polidori.
Trapped indoors, they read ghost stories aloud, and Byron proposed that each write one.
Mary struggled for days.
Polidori's effort became The Vampyre in 1819, which helped shape the vampire as an elegant aristocrat.
A waking dream.
After listening to Byron and Percy discuss whether life could be artificially created, Mary had what she later called a waking dream.
She pictured a pale student kneeling beside a thing he had put together, watching it stir into life, then fleeing in horror.
She described this in an introduction to the 1831 edition, so it is her own account, years later.
Mary was the daughter of two radical thinkers: Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, who died shortly after her birth, and the philosopher William Godwin.
Frankenstein was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was twenty.
Many reviewers assumed the author was a man.
Science at life's edge.
Frankenstein was not pure fantasy.
In the 1780s, the Italian scientist Luigi Galvani made the legs of dead frogs twitch using electricity, which led to the term galvanism.
His nephew Giovanni Aldini went further.
In London in 1803, he applied electric currents to the body of an executed criminal, making the face grimace and a hand rise, to the alarm of onlookers.
Many people wondered whether electricity might be the spark of life itself.
Mary Shelley knew about these debates.
In the novel, Victor Frankenstein is deliberately vague about his methods, but a scientist using cutting-edge knowledge to cross a forbidden line came straight from the science of her day.
The creature speaks.
Anyone who knows Frankenstein only from films may be surprised by the book.
First, Frankenstein is the scientist, Victor.
The creature is never given a name.
Second, he is no grunting brute.
Abandoned by his horrified creator, he teaches himself to speak and read by secretly watching a family through a gap in a cottage wall.
He reads Milton's Paradise Lost and compares himself to both Adam and Satan.
When he confronts Victor, he speaks with great eloquence about his loneliness and the cruelty he has suffered, and asks Victor to make him a companion.
Victor's refusal sets off the tragic final events.
The real horror of the book is rejection.
First science fiction.
Frankenstein grew out of the Gothic tradition of haunted castles, which began with Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764.
But Mary Shelley did something new.
Her monster was made not by a curse or spell but by a scientist using knowledge and method.
The writer Brian Aldiss argued this makes it the first true science fiction novel, a view many critics share.
The subtitle, The Modern Prometheus, points to the myth of the Titan who stole fire from the gods.
Her question was new: what responsibility do creators have for what they make?
The 1931 Universal film with Boris Karloff, and Jack Pierce's flat-topped makeup, turned the creature into a mostly silent icon.
The key idea: Frankenstein began in 1816, when a volcanic eruption's cold, stormy summer trapped young writers indoors.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did oral epics use repeated phrases like 'rosy-fingered Dawn'?
Answer. They helped singers remember the lines.
Question two. What made Shakespeare unusual among playwrights of his day?
Answer. He acted, wrote and part-owned a company.
Question three. Why is the title 'first novel' disputed?
Answer. It depends on how you define a novel.
Question four. What set the stage for the ghost story contest that produced Frankenstein?
Answer. A volcanic eruption cooled the climate and kept the group indoors.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
